modules.title: Triggers
modules.goal: Automate database-side reactions without hiding business logic or creating recursion.

topics.title: Trigger Basics
topics.simple: Trigger event par automatically chalne wala function hai.
topics.pro: A trigger binds a function to INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE or TRUNCATE events on a table.
points: It can run before or after the event.

example.sql: CREATE TRIGGER set_updated_at BEFORE UPDATE ON students FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION touch_updated_at();

topics.title: BEFORE Trigger
topics.simple: BEFORE trigger row change se pehle chalta hai.
topics.pro: A BEFORE trigger can validate or modify NEW before the row is written.
points: It runs once per affected row.

example.sql: CREATE TRIGGER validate_marks BEFORE INSERT OR UPDATE ON students FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION validate_marks();

topics.title: AFTER Trigger
topics.simple: AFTER trigger change ke baad chalta hai.
topics.pro: An AFTER trigger observes the committed row change and is used for auditing and side effects.
points: It cannot change NEW for the write.

example.sql: CREATE TRIGGER audit_students AFTER INSERT OR UPDATE OR DELETE ON students FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION audit_students();

topics.title: Row vs Statement Triggers
topics.simple: Row trigger har row par chalta hai; statement trigger ek baar.
topics.pro: FOR EACH ROW fires per affected row, while FOR EACH STATEMENT fires once per statement.
points: Statement triggers are cheaper for bulk work.
Transition tables work with statement triggers.

example.sql: CREATE TRIGGER audit_students AFTER UPDATE ON students FOR EACH STATEMENT EXECUTE FUNCTION audit_students();

topics.title: Trigger Function
topics.simple: Trigger function trigger context me chalta hai.
topics.pro: A trigger function returns trigger and uses NEW, OLD, TG_OP and TG_TABLE_NAME.
points: Return NULL to skip the operation.

example.sql: CREATE FUNCTION touch_updated_at() RETURNS trigger LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$ BEGIN NEW.updated_at = NOW(); RETURN NEW; END; $$;

topics.title: NEW and OLD
topics.simple: NEW naya row hai; OLD purana row.
topics.pro: NEW holds the proposed row for INSERT/UPDATE, OLD holds the previous row for UPDATE/DELETE.

example.sql: CREATE FUNCTION log_change() RETURNS trigger LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$ BEGIN RAISE NOTICE '% -> %', OLD.marks, NEW.marks; RETURN NEW; END; $$;

topics.title: Validation Trigger
topics.simple: Trigger complex validation kar sakta hai.
topics.pro: A trigger can enforce rules that span tables or need procedural logic beyond a CHECK constraint.

example.sql: CREATE FUNCTION require_email() RETURNS trigger LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$ BEGIN IF NEW.email IS NULL THEN RAISE EXCEPTION 'email required'; END IF; RETURN NEW; END; $$;

topics.title: Audit Trigger
topics.simple: Audit trigger changes ko history table me likhta hai.
topics.pro: An audit trigger records who changed what and when, usually in an append-only table.

example.sql: CREATE TABLE student_audit (id BIGINT GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY, student_id BIGINT, action TEXT, changed_at TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT NOW());

topics.title: Timestamp Trigger
topics.simple: Timestamp trigger updated_at maintain karta hai.
topics.pro: A BEFORE UPDATE trigger sets updated_at automatically so every writer gets the same behavior.
points: Do not rely on the app.

example.sql: CREATE FUNCTION touch_updated_at() RETURNS trigger LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$ BEGIN NEW.updated_at = NOW(); RETURN NEW; END; $$;

topics.title: Trigger Order
topics.simple: Same event par multiple triggers alphabetical order me chalte hain.
topics.pro: PostgreSQL fires triggers of the same kind in name order, so name them deliberately when order matters.

example.sql: CREATE TRIGGER a_validate BEFORE INSERT ON students FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION validate_marks();

topics.title: Enabling and Disabling
topics.simple: Trigger ko temporarily disable kar sakte hain.
topics.pro: ALTER TABLE ... DISABLE TRIGGER helps bulk loads but bypasses important rules.

example.sql: ALTER TABLE students DISABLE TRIGGER validate_marks;

topics.title: Dropping Triggers
topics.simple: DROP TRIGGER trigger hataata hai.
topics.pro: Drop the trigger before dropping its function, or use CASCADE deliberately.

example.sql: DROP TRIGGER IF EXISTS validate_marks ON students;

topics.title: Trigger vs Constraint
topics.simple: Simple rules constraints me rakho; complex side effects triggers me.
topics.pro: Constraints are declarative and optimized; triggers are procedural and easier to misuse.

example.sql: ALTER TABLE students ADD CONSTRAINT marks_range CHECK (marks BETWEEN 0 AND 100);

topics.title: Trigger Recursion
topics.simple: Trigger apne hi table par write karke recursion bana sakta hai.
topics.pro: A trigger that updates its own table can fire itself again; guard with conditions or a depth check.

example.sql: CREATE TRIGGER touch_updated_at BEFORE UPDATE ON students FOR EACH ROW WHEN (OLD.marks IS DISTINCT FROM NEW.marks) EXECUTE FUNCTION touch_updated_at();

topics.title: Trigger Performance
topics.simple: Row triggers bulk operations ko slow karte hain.
topics.pro: Every row trigger adds function-call and write overhead, especially during large updates.

example.sql: EXPLAIN ANALYZE UPDATE students SET marks = marks + 1;

topics.title: Common Trigger Errors
topics.simple: Missing RETURN, wrong timing aur recursion common errors hain.
topics.pro: Common failures are forgetting RETURN NEW, using AFTER to modify the row, and triggering an infinite update loop.
points: Return NEW in BEFORE row triggers.

example.sql: CREATE FUNCTION bad_trigger() RETURNS trigger LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$ BEGIN NEW.marks = 0; RETURN NEW; END; $$;

topics.title: Auditing
topics.simple: Audit trail append-only aur queryable hona chahiye.
topics.pro: A good audit table records the operation, key, before and after values, actor and timestamp.

example.sql: CREATE TABLE audit_log (id BIGINT GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY, table_name TEXT, action TEXT, row_data JSONB, changed_at TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT NOW());

topics.title: Trigger Security
topics.simple: Trigger function privileges carefully set karo.
topics.pro: Triggers run with the function owner’s privileges when SECURITY DEFINER is used, so validate inputs and fix search_path.

example.sql: CREATE FUNCTION audit_students() RETURNS trigger LANGUAGE plpgsql SECURITY DEFINER SET search_path = public AS $$ BEGIN INSERT INTO audit_log (table_name, action, row_data) VALUES (TG_TABLE_NAME, TG_OP, to_jsonb(NEW)); RETURN NEW; END; $$;

topics.title: Practical Trigger
topics.simple: updated_at aur audit trigger ko combine karo.
topics.pro: A practical trigger sets updated_at and writes an audit row in one controlled function.

example.sql: CREATE FUNCTION before_student_update() RETURNS trigger LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$ BEGIN NEW.updated_at = NOW(); INSERT INTO student_audit (student_id, action) VALUES (NEW.id, TG_OP); RETURN NEW; END; $$;

topics.title: Trigger Maintenance
topics.simple: Triggers ko version aur test karo.
topics.pro: Track trigger definitions, test them with bulk changes and review them during migrations.

example.sql: SELECT tgname, tgrelid::regclass FROM pg_trigger WHERE NOT tgisinternal;

interview.q: Module 25 · Explain Trigger Basics in a production query.
interview.answer: A trigger binds a function to INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE or TRUNCATE events on a table. Key rules: It runs automatically. It calls a trigger function. It can run before or after the event.

interview.q: Module 25 · Explain BEFORE Trigger in a production query.
interview.answer: A BEFORE trigger can validate or modify NEW before the row is written. Key rules: It can change NEW. It can reject the row. It runs once per affected row.

interview.q: Module 25 · Explain AFTER Trigger in a production query.
interview.answer: An AFTER trigger observes the committed row change and is used for auditing and side effects. Key rules: It sees the final row. It cannot change NEW for the write. It can queue more work.

interview.q: Module 25 · Explain Row vs Statement Triggers in a production query.
interview.answer: FOR EACH ROW fires per affected row, while FOR EACH STATEMENT fires once per statement. Key rules: Row triggers see NEW/OLD. Statement triggers are cheaper for bulk work. Transition tables work with statement triggers.

interview.q: Module 25 · Explain Trigger Function in a production query.
interview.answer: A trigger function returns trigger and uses NEW, OLD, TG_OP and TG_TABLE_NAME. Key rules: Return NEW for row triggers. Return NULL to skip the operation. Declare LANGUAGE plpgsql.

interview.q: Module 25 · Explain NEW and OLD in a production query.
interview.answer: NEW holds the proposed row for INSERT/UPDATE, OLD holds the previous row for UPDATE/DELETE. Key rules: INSERT has NEW only. DELETE has OLD only. UPDATE has both.

interview.q: Module 25 · Explain Validation Trigger in a production query.
interview.answer: A trigger can enforce rules that span tables or need procedural logic beyond a CHECK constraint. Key rules: Prefer CHECK for simple rules. Use triggers for cross-row rules. Raise a clear exception.

interview.q: Module 25 · Explain Audit Trigger in a production query.
interview.answer: An audit trigger records who changed what and when, usually in an append-only table. Key rules: Capture TG_OP. Store old and new values. Keep the audit insert durable.

interview.q: Module 25 · Explain Timestamp Trigger in a production query.
interview.answer: A BEFORE UPDATE trigger sets updated_at automatically so every writer gets the same behavior. Key rules: Set NEW.updated_at. Return NEW. Do not rely on the app.

interview.q: Module 25 · Explain Trigger Order in a production query.
interview.answer: PostgreSQL fires triggers of the same kind in name order, so name them deliberately when order matters. Key rules: Order is by name. Use BEFORE for validation. Use AFTER for side effects.

interview.q: Module 25 · Explain Enabling and Disabling in a production query.
interview.answer: ALTER TABLE ... DISABLE TRIGGER helps bulk loads but bypasses important rules. Key rules: Disable only during controlled maintenance. Re-enable immediately. Foreign-key triggers are special.

interview.q: Module 25 · Explain Dropping Triggers in a production query.
interview.answer: Drop the trigger before dropping its function, or use CASCADE deliberately. Key rules: Name the table and trigger. IF EXISTS is script-safe. The function remains until dropped.

interview.q: Module 25 · Explain Trigger vs Constraint in a production query.
interview.answer: Constraints are declarative and optimized; triggers are procedural and easier to misuse. Key rules: Prefer constraints. Use triggers for auditing. Document every trigger.

interview.q: Module 25 · Explain Trigger Recursion in a production query.
interview.answer: A trigger that updates its own table can fire itself again; guard with conditions or a depth check. Key rules: Avoid self-updates. Use WHEN clauses. Test the recursion path.

interview.q: Module 25 · Explain Trigger Performance in a production query.
interview.answer: Every row trigger adds function-call and write overhead, especially during large updates. Key rules: Prefer set-based SQL. Use statement triggers when possible. Measure bulk loads.

interview.q: Module 25 · Explain Common Trigger Errors in a production query.
interview.answer: Common failures are forgetting RETURN NEW, using AFTER to modify the row, and triggering an infinite update loop. Key rules: Return NEW in BEFORE row triggers. Use BEFORE to modify. Guard recursion.

interview.q: Module 25 · Explain Auditing in a production query.
interview.answer: A good audit table records the operation, key, before and after values, actor and timestamp. Key rules: Record the actor. Store before/after. Never update audit rows.

interview.q: Module 25 · Explain Trigger Security in a production query.
interview.answer: Triggers run with the function owner’s privileges when SECURITY DEFINER is used, so validate inputs and fix search_path. Key rules: Avoid SECURITY DEFINER by default. Set search_path. Do not trust NEW blindly.

interview.q: Module 25 · Explain Practical Trigger in a production query.
interview.answer: A practical trigger sets updated_at and writes an audit row in one controlled function. Key rules: Set the timestamp first. Write the audit row. Return the final NEW.

interview.q: Module 25 · Explain Trigger Maintenance in a production query.
interview.answer: Track trigger definitions, test them with bulk changes and review them during migrations. Key rules: List triggers per table. Test with multi-row statements. Drop obsolete triggers.

logic.answer: FOR EACH ROW fires per affected row, while FOR EACH STATEMENT fires once per statement. Row triggers see NEW/OLD. Statement triggers are cheaper for bulk work. Transition tables work with statement triggers.

logic.q: Module 25 · Why does Trigger Function matter?
logic.answer: A trigger function returns trigger and uses NEW, OLD, TG_OP and TG_TABLE_NAME. Return NEW for row triggers. Return NULL to skip the operation. Declare LANGUAGE plpgsql.

logic.q: Module 25 · Why does NEW and OLD matter?
logic.answer: NEW holds the proposed row for INSERT/UPDATE, OLD holds the previous row for UPDATE/DELETE. INSERT has NEW only. DELETE has OLD only. UPDATE has both.

logic.q: Module 25 · Why does Validation Trigger matter?
logic.answer: A trigger can enforce rules that span tables or need procedural logic beyond a CHECK constraint. Prefer CHECK for simple rules. Use triggers for cross-row rules. Raise a clear exception.

logic.q: Module 25 · Why does Audit Trigger matter?
logic.answer: An audit trigger records who changed what and when, usually in an append-only table. Capture TG_OP. Store old and new values. Keep the audit insert durable.

logic.q: Module 25 · Why does Timestamp Trigger matter?
logic.answer: A BEFORE UPDATE trigger sets updated_at automatically so every writer gets the same behavior. Set NEW.updated_at. Return NEW. Do not rely on the app.

logic.q: Module 25 · Why does Trigger Order matter?
logic.answer: PostgreSQL fires triggers of the same kind in name order, so name them deliberately when order matters. Order is by name. Use BEFORE for validation. Use AFTER for side effects.

logic.q: Module 25 · Why does Enabling and Disabling matter?
logic.answer: ALTER TABLE ... DISABLE TRIGGER helps bulk loads but bypasses important rules. Disable only during controlled maintenance. Re-enable immediately. Foreign-key triggers are special.

logic.q: Module 25 · Why does Dropping Triggers matter?
logic.answer: Drop the trigger before dropping its function, or use CASCADE deliberately. Name the table and trigger. IF EXISTS is script-safe. The function remains until dropped.

logic.q: Module 25 · Why does Trigger vs Constraint matter?
logic.answer: Constraints are declarative and optimized; triggers are procedural and easier to misuse. Prefer constraints. Use triggers for auditing. Document every trigger.

logic.q: Module 25 · Why does Trigger Recursion matter?
logic.answer: A trigger that updates its own table can fire itself again; guard with conditions or a depth check. Avoid self-updates. Use WHEN clauses. Test the recursion path.

logic.q: Module 25 · Why does Trigger Performance matter?
logic.answer: Every row trigger adds function-call and write overhead, especially during large updates. Prefer set-based SQL. Use statement triggers when possible. Measure bulk loads.

debug.title: Missing RETURN
debug.broken: CREATE FUNCTION touch() RETURNS trigger LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$ BEGIN NEW.updated_at = NOW(); END; $$;
debug.fix: CREATE FUNCTION touch() RETURNS trigger LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$ BEGIN NEW.updated_at = NOW(); RETURN NEW; END; $$;
debug.error: control reached end of trigger procedure without RETURN

debug.title: AFTER cannot modify
debug.broken: CREATE TRIGGER t AFTER UPDATE ON students FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION touch_updated_at();
debug.fix: CREATE TRIGGER t BEFORE UPDATE ON students FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION touch_updated_at();
debug.error: NEW changes in an AFTER trigger do not affect the stored row
debug.expected: The timestamp is set before writing.

debug.title: Row trigger on truncate
debug.broken: CREATE TRIGGER t BEFORE TRUNCATE ON students FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION touch();
debug.fix: CREATE TRIGGER t BEFORE TRUNCATE ON students FOR EACH STATEMENT EXECUTE FUNCTION touch();
debug.error: TRUNCATE does not support FOR EACH ROW

debug.title: Recursive update
debug.broken: CREATE TRIGGER t AFTER UPDATE ON students FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION update_student();
debug.fix: Add a WHEN condition or a guard column so the trigger does not update the same row again.

debug.title: Wrong trigger return
debug.broken: CREATE FUNCTION f() RETURNS trigger LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$ BEGIN RETURN NULL; END; $$;
debug.fix: Return NEW when the row should proceed.

debug.title: Missing function
debug.broken: CREATE TRIGGER t BEFORE UPDATE ON students FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION missing_fn();
debug.fix:
CREATE FUNCTION missing_fn() RETURNS trigger LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$ BEGIN RETURN NEW; END; $$;
CREATE TRIGGER t BEFORE UPDATE ON students FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION missing_fn();

debug.title: Trigger name collision
debug.broken:
CREATE TRIGGER t BEFORE UPDATE ON students FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION touch();
CREATE TRIGGER t BEFORE INSERT ON students FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION touch();
debug.fix: Use distinct trigger names for each event.

debug.title: Audit without actor
debug.fix: INSERT INTO audit_log (action, actor) VALUES (TG_OP, current_user);
debug.error: The audit row cannot identify who changed the data

debug.title: Disable forgotten
debug.broken: ALTER TABLE students DISABLE TRIGGER validate_marks;
debug.fix: ALTER TABLE students ENABLE TRIGGER validate_marks;

debug.title: Drop function first
debug.fix:
DROP TRIGGER touch_updated_at ON students;
DROP FUNCTION touch_updated_at();
debug.error: cannot drop function because other objects depend on it
